alt.origin: Laboratory limits are conventionally the central 95% of a “healthy” reference group; for ALT, such groups historically included individuals with undiagnosed fatty liver and were assembled without regard to BMI, and a survey of 67 laboratories in one US state found upper reference limits from 31 to 72 U/L, set variously from manufacturer inserts, local controls or textbooks [S2]. LabCorp derived its current limits (female <33, male <45 U/L) from an internal study of more than 260,000 subjects and cites Prati et al. (2002) as a reason for lowering them [S4]; the Leeds NHS trust uses a Siemens insert traced to a 2000 textbook [S7]; the Australasian harmonised limits (male 40, female 35 U/L) were confirmed against 1,876 healthy adults [S9].
alt.sexSpecificWhat: ACG 2017 “true healthy normal” upper limit of ALT (range quoted as 19 to 25 U/L in women, 29 to 33 U/L in men); higher values should be assessed
alt.contestedSummary: Prati et al. (2002), in 6,835 screened blood donors in Milan, set the 95th-percentile upper reference limit at 30 U/L in men and 19 U/L in women against the then-current 40 and 30 U/L; the new limits raised sensitivity for HCV viraemia from 55% to 76.3% [S1]. Ruhl and Everhart (2012), in NHANES (3,747 low-risk versus 259 HCV-positive participants), found optimal cut-offs of 29 U/L in men and 22 U/L in women, which would classify 28.3% of US women as “elevated” [S3]. The American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) 2017 guideline adopted 19 to 25 U/L for women, whereas laboratories still report upper limits of 33 to 50 U/L, and the 2021 repetition of the Prati study (21,296 donors) with an assay standardised to the International Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine (IFCC) method gave 30 U/L for women because the standardised assay yields higher values [S10, S11].
alt.guidanceInBand: The American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) 2017 guideline states: “A normal ALT should be <29-33 IU/l in males and 19-25 IU/l in females. Minimal elevations may be approached by a history and examination, discontinuation of hepatotoxic medicines and all alcohol consumption, in addition to an evaluation for hemochromatosis, fatty liver and viral hepatitis.” A borderline elevation is “<2X ULN”; for levels below 5 times the upper reference limit, the history and tests “should assess for viral hepatitis B and C, alcoholic and NAFLD, hemochromatosis, Wilson's disease, alpha-1-anti-trypsin deficiency, autoimmune hepatitis and consider drugs/supplement related injury” (strong recommendation, very low level of evidence) [S2].
alt.labRangeSource: LabCorp (female <33, male <45 U/L, adults aged 18 and over); ARUP reports 5 to 50 U/L “by report”; Leeds NHS adults <=40 U/L (not sex-specific); RCPA/AACB harmonised male 5 to 40, female 5 to 35 U/L

ast.origin: The International Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine (IFCC) multicentre reference study (765 adults, 411 women) found a sex difference in AST upper limits of 1.7 U/L and therefore defined a single interval of 11 to 34 U/L [S12]; the Leeds NHS trust adopts this as <35 U/L [S7]. The Australasian harmonisation committee nevertheless adopted sex-specific limits, 5 to 35 U/L in men and 5 to 30 U/L in women, confirmed against 1,876 healthy adults [S9]. The American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) states that AST and ALT ranges “can vary between different labs” and works in multiples of the local upper limit [S2].
ast.sexSpecificWhat: Harmonised laboratory upper reference limit (RCPA/AACB, Australia and New Zealand); no clinical guideline sets a sex-specific AST threshold
ast.contestedSummary: Reference studies disagree on whether AST requires sex-specific limits: the International Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine (IFCC) study found a sex difference of 1.7 U/L and used one interval, 11 to 34 U/L [S12], whereas RCPA/AACB adopted 35 U/L for men and 30 U/L for women [S9]. The American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) cites a German cohort in which AST >18 U/L was associated with 3-fold all-cause mortality and a Korean cohort in which AST of 30 to 39 IU/L was associated with 8-fold liver-related death risk versus <20 IU/L, which places the upper limit of every laboratory range within a risk gradient [S2].
ast.guidanceInBand: The American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) 2017 guideline states: “A borderline AST and/or ALT elevation is defined as <2X ULN”; for levels below 5 times the upper reference limit, “the history and laboratory testing should assess for viral hepatitis B and C, alcoholic and NAFLD, hemochromatosis, Wilson's disease, alpha-1-anti-trypsin deficiency, autoimmune hepatitis and consider drugs/supplement related injury” [S2].
ast.labRangeSource: RCPA/AACB harmonised via Alfred Health (male <35, female <30 U/L); Leeds NHS <35 U/L for all adults; LabCorp reports no interval on its test page

ggt.origin: The International Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine (IFCC) multicentre study derived GGT intervals of 6 to 40 U/L in women and 12 to 68 U/L in men after excluding Nordic samples, whose upper limits were higher, and concluded that a worldwide common GGT interval “appears unlikely due to differences among populations” [S12]; the Leeds NHS trust uses these intervals unchanged [S7]. The Australasian committee noted that “Most data sets show male activities are greater than for females” and set 5 to 50 U/L for men and 5 to 35 U/L for women [S9]. The derivation of the LabCorp limits (0 to 65 and 0 to 60 IU/L) is not stated on its test page [S15].
ggt.sexSpecificWhat: Harmonised laboratory upper reference limit (RCPA/AACB); the IFCC study gives 40 (women) and 68 U/L (men); no clinical guideline sets a sex-specific GGT threshold
ggt.contestedSummary: Screened reference populations placed the female upper reference limit at 35 to 40 U/L [S9, S12], whereas LabCorp reports up to 60 U/L, 5 U/L below its male limit [S15]; a value of 50 U/L in a woman therefore falls within the LabCorp reference interval and above the upper limit of the NHS trust and the Australian laboratories consulted. The International Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine (IFCC) study authors found that GGT limits differ by region, so the female limit is population-dependent [S12].
ggt.guidanceInBand: Recommendation 13 of the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) 2017 guideline states: “An elevation of alkaline phosphatase should be confirmed with an elevation in GGT. Given its lack of specificity for liver disease, GGT should not be used as a screening test for underlying liver disease in the absence of other abnormal liver chemistries. (Strong recommendation, very low level of evidence)” [S2].
ggt.labRangeSource: LabCorp (female 0 to 60, male 0 to 65 IU/L); Leeds NHS female 6 to 40, male 12 to 68 U/L; RCPA/AACB harmonised female 5 to 35, male 5 to 50 U/L

alp.origin: Single adult intervals derive from national harmonisation projects: UK Pathology Harmony 2011 (30 to 130 U/L, used by the Leeds NHS trust) [S7] and the AACB 2014 endorsement (30 to 110 U/L, confirmed against 1,876 healthy adults) [S9]; paediatric sex- and age-specific intervals derive from CALIPER [S7]. The American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) states that clinicians “may rely on local lab ULN ranges for alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin” because replication of ALP ranges across laboratories “has not been reported as problematic” [S2]. The NHS trust database notes that ALP “changes quite markedly throughout life with peaks in childhood and puberty (and pregnancy)” [S7].
alp.sexSpecificWhat: LabCorp upper reference limit at ages 51 to 80 (female limit exceeds male limit after 50); laboratory table only, no guideline threshold
alp.contestedSummary: No published argument that the adult female ALP limit is derived from an inappropriate reference population was identified. The sex-relevant observations are that the LabCorp female upper limit rises above the male limit after age 50 (135 versus 123 IU/L), whereas single-interval laboratories apply one limit to all adults [S17 vs S7, S9], and that pregnancy raises ALP physiologically [S7].
alp.guidanceInBand: The American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) 2017 guideline states: “An elevation of alkaline phosphatase should be confirmed with an elevation in GGT”; evaluation branches at “alkaline phosphatase 1-2x ULN” versus “> 2x ULN”, and anti-mitochondrial antibody testing for PBC and MR cholangiography/ERCP with IgG4 for PSC are recommended for hepatic ALP elevation [S2].
alp.labRangeSource: LabCorp adults 21 to 50 years (female 41 to 116, male 47 to 123 IU/L; 51 to 80 years: female 49 to 135, male 47 to 123 IU/L); Leeds NHS adult 30 to 130 U/L (Pathology Harmony); RCPA/AACB adult 30 to 110 U/L

hba1c.origin: These are diagnostic decision thresholds, not population reference intervals. The American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care 2026 define diabetes in Table 2.1 as “A1C >=6.5% (>=48 mmol/mol)” and prediabetes in Table 2.2 as “A1C 5.7-6.4% (39-47 mmol/mol)”, and require an NGSP-certified assay standardised to the DCCT [S18]; the Leeds NHS trust uses the WHO 2011 limit of 48 mmol/mol and a local non-diabetic cut-off of <42 mmol/mol [S7]. The ADA notes that “Black individuals have slightly higher A1C levels (approximately 0.3%)” and that in conditions with altered red cell turnover, pregnancy, some haemoglobin variants, G6PD deficiency and HIV, “plasma glucose criteria should be used to diagnose diabetes” [S18].
hba1c.sexSpecificWhat: No guideline or laboratory consulted sets a sex-specific HbA1c threshold
hba1c.contestedSummary: Holland et al. (2024), in 146,907 UK adults with a single test (replicated in 938,678 from six laboratories), found that women under 50 had a mean HbA1c of 34.4 versus 36.0 mmol/mol in men (1.6 mmol/mol lower, p < 0.0001; 0.9 mmol/mol at 50 and over); the authors modelled lowering the diagnostic cut-off from 48 to 46 mmol/mol (6.5% to 6.4%) for women under 50, estimated that 34,953 additional women in England and Wales would be reclassified, and attributed the difference to “menstruation and hence shorter erythrocyte survival” (about 4% of circulating blood, approximately 1.9 mmol/mol) [S21]. The mechanism is inferred, and no guideline has adopted a sex-specific cut-off.
hba1c.guidanceInBand: The American Diabetes Association (ADA) 2026 standards define prediabetes as “A1C 5.7-6.4% (39-47 mmol/mol)” and diabetes as “A1C >=6.5% (>=48 mmol/mol)”; in the absence of unequivocal hyperglycaemia a confirmatory test is required [S18]. LabCorp states “Prediabetes: 5.7% to 6.4%” and that patients with prediabetes should be retested yearly [S19].
hba1c.labRangeSource: LabCorp (4.8 to 5.6%; prediabetes 5.7 to 6.4%; diabetes >=6.5%); Leeds NHS <42 mmol/mol, diabetes >48 mmol/mol

glucose_fasting.origin: These are decision thresholds of the American Diabetes Association (ADA): Table 2.1 defines diabetes as “FPG >=126 mg/dL (>=7.0 mmol/L)” and Table 2.2 prediabetes as “FPG 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) to 125 mg/dL (6.9 mmol/L) (IFG)”, with the definition “Fasting is defined as no caloric intake for at least 8 h” [S18]. The Leeds NHS trust uses the WHO 2006 criteria: impaired fasting glucose at 6.1 to 6.9 mmol/L and diabetes at 7.0 mmol/L or above [S7]. LabCorp notes that fasting glucose “tends to be higher in the morning than in the afternoon” [S20].
glucose_fasting.sexSpecificWhat: No sex-specific fasting glucose threshold in ADA 2026, WHO-based NHS ranges or LabCorp
glucose_fasting.contestedSummary: No study addressing sex differences in fasting glucose distributions was identified. The only verified sex-related statement is the instruction of the American Diabetes Association (ADA) that, in pregnancy and in conditions altering red cell turnover, plasma glucose rather than A1C should be used for diagnosis [S18].
glucose_fasting.guidanceInBand: The American Diabetes Association (ADA) 2026 standards define “FPG 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) to 125 mg/dL (6.9 mmol/L) (IFG)” as prediabetes; diabetes requires “FPG >=126 mg/dL (>=7.0 mmol/L)”, with confirmation in the absence of unequivocal hyperglycaemia [S18].
glucose_fasting.labRangeSource: LabCorp (70 to 99 mg/dL); Leeds NHS fasting 3.5 to 6.0 mmol/L

total_cholesterol.origin: The decision thresholds are reproduced from Table 2 of the National Cholesterol Education Program Adult Treatment Panel III (NCEP ATP III, 2001): total cholesterol “<200 Desirable; 200-239 Borderline high; >=240 High” [S22]. ATP III is an expert-panel classification built on LDL as the primary target; the NHS trust database reports no range and refers to risk calculators [S7].
total_cholesterol.sexSpecificWhat: No sex-specific total cholesterol threshold in ATP III, ESC/EAS 2019 or the laboratories consulted
total_cholesterol.contestedSummary: The BioCycle study (259 women aged 18 to 44, up to 16 visits over two cycles) found that median total cholesterol varied from 166 mg/dL (mid-follicular) to 157 mg/dL (late luteal), with a within-woman mean change of 19% (27.7 mg/dL) over the cycle; 14.3% of women were at or above 200 mg/dL at mid-follicular versus 7.9% at late luteal visits, and 19.7% exceeded 200 mg/dL at least once but 5% did so at every visit [S24]. The authors state that measurements “should be appropriately timed to menstrual cycle phase” [S24]; no guideline consulted addresses this.
total_cholesterol.guidanceInBand: The Adult Treatment Panel III (ATP III) classifies “200-239 Borderline high”; where non-fasting total cholesterol is 200 mg/dL or above, “a followup lipoprotein profile is needed for appropriate management based on LDL” [S22]. No guideline text on cycle timing was identified; the BioCycle authors recommend standardising the timing of lipid measurement [S24].
total_cholesterol.labRangeSource: LabCorp (over 19 years: acceptable <200 (or 100 to 199); borderline 200 to 239; high >=240 mg/dL)

ldl.origin: Table 2 of the Adult Treatment Panel III (ATP III) classifies LDL as “<100 Optimal; 100-129 Near optimal/above optimal; 130-159 Borderline high; 160-189 High; >=190 Very high”, with treatment goals set by risk category [S22]. The European Society of Cardiology/European Atherosclerosis Society (ESC/EAS) 2019 guideline replaces categories with risk-based LDL-C goals [S31]. The NHS trust calculates LDL as “Total chol - HDL - (trigs/2.29)” and reports no range [S7].
ldl.sexSpecificWhat: No sex-specific LDL threshold in ATP III, ESC/EAS 2019 or the laboratories consulted; the 2018 AHA/ACC guideline adds women-specific risk enhancers (premature menopause, pre-eclampsia) rather than lipid thresholds, according to a 2020 review in Circulation [S33]
ldl.contestedSummary: In the BioCycle study, median LDL was 102 mg/dL (mid-follicular) versus 96 mg/dL (late luteal), and 17.8% of women were at or above 130 mg/dL at mid-follicular versus 10.5% at late luteal visits; “Total and LDL cholesterol were lower during the luteal phase as compared with the follicular phase” [S24]. The European Society of Cardiology/European Atherosclerosis Society (ESC/EAS) guideline notes that “women have not been adequately represented in statin trials” [S31].
ldl.guidanceInBand: The Adult Treatment Panel III (ATP III) classifies “100-129 Near optimal/above optimal” and “130-159 Borderline high”; for 0 to 1 risk factors the LDL goal is <160 mg/dL and lifestyle change starts at 160 mg/dL or above [S22]. The European Society of Cardiology/European Atherosclerosis Society (ESC/EAS) 2019 guideline links the LDL-C goal to estimated risk and recommends statins “for primary prevention in high-risk women” with the same goals as in men [S31].
ldl.labRangeSource: LabCorp direct LDL (over 19 years: 0 to 99 mg/dL, same for male and female)

hdl.origin: The National Cholesterol Education Program Adult Treatment Panel III (NCEP ATP III, 2001) raised “categorical low HDL cholesterol from <35 mg/dL to <40 mg/dL because the latter is a better measure of a depressed HDL” and set it “both in men and women” [S22, S23]. The panel explained that women “typically have higher HDL cholesterol levels than men”, so that <40 mg/dL identifies “approximately one-third of men and about one-fifth of women”, and that “Setting a different cutpoint for categorical low HDL cholesterol for men and women was rejected because it would make many women who are otherwise at low risk eligible for LDL-lowering drugs”; instead, “<50 mg/dL” was made “a marginal risk factor in women”, used only in the metabolic syndrome definition [S23]. The LabCorp limit of “>39” reproduces the ATP III categorical value for all patients [S27].
hdl.sexSpecificWhat: Low HDL-C criterion for the metabolic syndrome (ATP III Table 8: men <40 mg/dL, women <50 mg/dL; three of five criteria establish the diagnosis)
hdl.contestedSummary: The Adult Treatment Panel III (ATP III) report records that the female cut-point was a policy compromise: <50 mg/dL was “rejected” as a categorical risk factor to avoid making “many women who are otherwise at low risk eligible for LDL-lowering drugs”, and retained only as a “marginal risk factor” in the metabolic syndrome criteria [S23]. Laboratories in turn report a single limit (LabCorp >39 mg/dL for all [S27]; University of Washington, female >=50 mg/dL [S30]); a value of 45 mg/dL in a woman falls within the reference interval of the first and below the lower reference limit of the second. In the BioCycle study, HDL also varied with the cycle, from a median of 48 mg/dL at menses to 52 mg/dL at ovulation (“HDL levels were highest around ovulation”) [S24]. The current European Society of Cardiology/European Atherosclerosis Society (ESC/EAS) 2019 guideline sets no HDL goal: “To date, no specific goals for HDL-C or TG levels have been determined in clinical trials” and HDL-raising therapies “do not reduce the risk of ASCVD” [S31]; according to Agarwala et al. (2020) [S33], the women-specific additions of the 2018 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) guideline are risk enhancers (premature menopause, pre-eclampsia), not an HDL threshold (reported in a secondary source; guideline full text not verified).
hdl.guidanceInBand: The Adult Treatment Panel III (ATP III) does not count a value in this band as a risk factor (“Low HDL cholesterol (<40 mg/dL)”) [S22], but “for women, HDL cholesterol <50 mg/dL counts as one indicator in the diagnosis of the metabolic syndrome”, “a marginal risk factor in women, which will mandate more intensive lifestyle therapies (weight reduction and increased physical activity)” [S23]; metabolic syndrome is diagnosed “when three or more of the risk determinants shown in Table 8 are present” [S22]. The European Society of Cardiology/European Atherosclerosis Society (ESC/EAS) 2019 guideline sets no HDL-C goal [S31].
hdl.labRangeSource: LabCorp (>39 mg/dL, one interval for all); University of Washington Medicine reports male >=40, female >=50 mg/dL

S32.title: 2018 AHA/ACC Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol
S32.note: Bibliographic record consulted; full text not verified.

S34.title: Diagnosis and management of the metabolic syndrome: AHA/NHLBI Scientific Statement
S34.note: Bibliographic record consulted; full text not verified.

S35.title: Harmonizing the metabolic syndrome: a joint interim statement

triglycerides.origin: The Adult Treatment Panel III (ATP III) lowered the triglyceride categories of ATP II to “Normal <150 mg/dL; Borderline-high 150-199; High 200-499; Very high >=500” (ATP II: <200, 200 to 399, 400 to 1000, >1000) “to give more attention to moderate elevations” [S22, S23]; a value of 150 mg/dL or above is also one of the five metabolic syndrome criteria [S22]. The NHS trust fasting limit of <2.3 mmol/L derives from the 1987 European Atherosclerosis Society recommendations [S7].
triglycerides.sexSpecificWhat: No sex-specific triglyceride threshold in ATP III, ESC/EAS 2019 or the laboratories consulted
triglycerides.contestedSummary: In the BioCycle study, median triglycerides were 56 mg/dL (mid-follicular) versus 49 mg/dL (late luteal), lowest immediately before menstruation [S24, S25]; the within-woman variation is small relative to the 150 mg/dL cut-off. The Adult Treatment Panel III (ATP III) notes that when triglycerides exceed 150 mg/dL, HDL concentrations “frequently are <40 mg/dL in men (or <50 mg/dL in women)” [S23]. No evidence that the female threshold is inappropriately set was identified.
triglycerides.guidanceInBand: The Adult Treatment Panel III (ATP III) classifies “150-199 Borderline-high”; the panel “Recommends treatment beyond LDL lowering for persons with triglycerides >=200 mg/dL” and for the metabolic syndrome stresses “weight reduction and increased physical activity” [S22]. The European Society of Cardiology/European Atherosclerosis Society (ESC/EAS) 2019 guideline states that no specific triglyceride goal has been determined in clinical trials [S31].
triglycerides.labRangeSource: LabCorp (normal <150; borderline-high 150 to 199; high 200 to 499; very high >500 mg/dL); Leeds NHS fasting <2.3 mmol/L
